# Exploring the interplay among artificial intelligence literacy, creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement in college students: Findings from PLS-SEM and FsQCA

**Zhu Chun**[^1]** · Yimin Ning**[^2] [** ·**](http://orcid.org/0000-0002-6491-0906) **Jihe Chen**[^3]** · Tommy Tanu Wijaya**[^4]

Received: 12 February 2025 / Accepted: 9 May 2025 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2025

**Abstract** With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence technology, the artificial intel- ligence literacy, creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement of college stu- dents have increasingly garnered attention from the global educational community. This study, based on cognitive behavioral theory, employs Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to explore the interplay among these constructs. Data were col- lected from 385 Chinese college students. PLS-SEM results show that artificial intelligence literacy directly affects academic achievement and indirectly enhances it through self-efficacy and creativity. It also directly influences self-efficacy and indirectly promotes it via creativity. Creativity directly impacts academic achieve- ment and indirectly strengthens it through self-efficacy. Furthermore, artificial in- telligence literacy positively affects creativity, which in turn positively influences self-efficacy, ultimately benefiting academic achievement. fsQCA analysis reveals that academic achievement, self-efficacy, and creativity are influenced by multiple factors, with artificial intelligence literacy as a core condition in all effective con- figurations. These findings provide empirical evidence for understanding the core competencies required by college students in the age of artificial intelligence and offer practical guidance for cultivating future talents.

**Keywords** Artificial intelligence literacy · Self-efficacy · Creativity · Academic achievement · Cognitive behavioral theory

 Yimin Ning

**1 Introduction**

Amidst the swift progression of artificial intelligence(AI), an increasing emphasis is being placed on the AI literacy, self-efficacy, creativity, and academic achievement of university students in the global educational landscape (Chen et al., 2024b). The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) has underscored the challenges and opportunities that AI poses in the realm of educa- tion, as delineated in its report titled _Artificial Intelligence in Education: Challenges and Opportunities for Sustainable Development_ (UNESCO, 2023). Additionally, the pivotal role of AI literacy and skills has been accentuated within the _Beijing Con-_ _sensus on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Education_ (UNESCO, 2019), underscoring their significance in shaping the future of education. The Programme for Interna- tional Student Assessment (PISA) has positioned creative competencies at the heart of educational priorities, as indicated in the OECD’s, 2024 report (OECD, 2024). Similarly, the World Economic Forum’s _The Future of Jobs Report 2023_ projects an increased demand for skills such as creativity and self-efficacy in the evolving work- place landscape (WEF, 2023).In alignment with these global trends, the Ministry of Education in Singapore has integrated digital skills and literacy into its curriculum through the _Transforming Education through Technology_ Masterplan 2030, aiming to equip students with the necessary competencies for a digitalized world (MOE, 2023). In this context, AI literacy becomes the foundation for college students to understand and apply AI technologies, while self-efficacy serves as the driving force for their continuous development and adaptation to changes. Creativity is key to their problem-solving and innovation. These competencies and abilities are interwoven, collectively influencing the academic achievement of college students (Zhou et al., 2024).

AI literacy, self-efficacy, creativity, and academic achievement among university students have become essential metrics for evaluating the adaptability and quality of higher education (Yao et al., 2023).Despite the growing importance and scrutiny of these competencies, research reveals that university students’ performance in these domains is still lacking. The deficiency in artificial AI literacy among university stu- dents has emerged as an increasingly prominent issue. In the era of AI, it is impera- tive for students to acquire knowledge and skills related to AI technologies (Zhang et al., 2022b). However, research indicates that many university students exhibit sig- nificant shortcomings in both AI knowledge and application skills, which restricts their capabilities in innovation and problem-solving (Ma et al., 2024b). Furthermore, inadequate self-efficacy has profound implications for students’ academic perfor- mance and mental health. Self-efficacy, defined as an individual’s confidence in their abilities, has a direct impact on students’ motivation and achievement (Beghetto, [2006)](#declarations). Studies have shown that university students with low self-efficacy may lack confidence when facing challenges, which not only affects their academic success but also poses barriers to their career development (Xu et al., 2022). Although creativity is recognized as a core skill for the 21 st century, its cultivation is often marginalized within educational systems, resulting in students lacking the necessary innovative thinking and problem-solving abilities when confronted with new challenges (Ting & Yeh, 2023). Ultimately, insufficient academic achievement directly impacts stu-

dents’ future career prospects. Academic achievement serves as a critical indicator of students’ performance; however, many university students fail to meet their expected goals in terms of academic grades and skill acquisition (Wang et al., 2024). This not only affects their personal growth and development but also limits their capacity to contribute significantly to societal and economic advancement.

Although existing research has addressed factors such as students’ AI literacy, self-efficacy, creativity, and academic achievement, there is a scarcity of studies that simultaneously examine the interrelationships among these variables. Most studies focus on one or two variables, lacking a comprehensive exploration of their combined effects. Furthermore, empirical research integrating Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and Fuzzy Set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to investigate these variables is limited. The combination of these two meth- odologies can provide a more holistic analytical perspective, revealing the complex relationships and interaction effects among the variables. Therefore, this study aims to employ both methodologies to explore the relationships between college students’ AI literacy and their creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement, with the goal of offering insights for curriculum design and teaching practices in the field of AI education, ultimately fostering talent that meets the demands of future society.

**2 Literature review**

**2.1 Cognitive behavioral theory**

In this study, Cognitive Behavioral Theory (CBT) is utilized as the theoretical frame- work to explore the relationships among college students’ AI literacy, creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement. CBT emphasizes the interplay between cognition, emotion, and behavior. AI literacy, as a cognitive dimension, can effec- tively enhance students’ self-efficacy. This enhancement arises from a deeper under- standing and mastery of AI technologies, which empowers students with greater confidence to tackle and resolve tasks in related fields (Kariri & Almubaddel, 2024). Further research reveals that creativity also serves as a critical cognitive element that significantly promotes self-efficacy, as creativity is regarded as a core competency for solving complex problems and addressing challenges (Ebadi & Amini, 2024). The positive impact of self-efficacy on academic achievement becomes a crucial link within the research framework, as its enhancement can motivate students to engage more actively in their learning, thereby improving their academic performance (Mamlok, 2024). Moreover, the positive impact of AI literacy on academic achieve- ment has been empirically supported, as a deeper understanding of technology can significantly enhance students’ performance in their specialized courses (Chou et al., 2024). Creativity is closely linked to students’ personalized interests and hob- bies, suggesting its important role in academic success (Dong, 2021). This study also considers the different aspects of AI literacy and creativity as cognitive dimensions, highlighting their intrinsic connections, which can be realized through the dynamic transformation of knowledge and thought (Kariri & Almubaddel, 2024). Therefore, the model we constructed views AI literacy as a critical factor influencing individual creativity, providing the necessary knowledge to further enhance creativity and prob- lem-solving abilities.

In selecting the theoretical framework, this study considered various theories, including Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) and Self-Determination Theory (SDT). SCT focuses on the interplay between personal factors, behavior, and environmental influences (Bandura, [1986)](#declarations). However, it primarily addresses external influences and may not fully capture the internal cognitive processes and self-regulatory mecha- nisms that drive the relationships among AI literacy, creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement. SDT emphasizes intrinsic and extrinsic motivation (Deci & Ryan, 2000), but it does not directly address the core cognitive, affective, and behav- ioral dynamics of this study.

Given the limitations of these theories, this study ultimately chose CBT. CBT provides a comprehensive understanding of how cognitive factors influence behavior and performance, has a strong empirical basis, and has been widely applied in edu- cational research to explain how cognitive processes affect learning outcomes. This makes CBT the most appropriate framework for examining this study.

**2.2 Artificial intelligence literacy**

In the exploration of the relationships between college students’ AI literacy and their creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement, existing research has made sig- nificant strides. AI literacy among college students is recognized as a pivotal factor in shaping academic experiences and future opportunities (Toker Gokce et al., 2024). This literacy encompasses not only students’ understanding of AI technology but also their application and creation of AI technology (Walter, 2024). In this context, research has investigated the impact of various factors on AI literacy, including gen- der, frequency of AI application use, completion of AI-related courses, and fields of study (Shen & Cui, 2024; Toker Gokce et al., 2024). To comprehensively assess this literacy, researchers have developed the “AI Literacy Scale for Chinese College Students” (AILS-CCS), which quantifies students’ AI knowledge and skills and mea- sures their development across four key dimensions: cognitive, affective, behavioral, and ethical (Ma & Chen, 2024). Studies have also emphasized the cultivation of students’ AI literacy through teaching experimental interventions, such as providing specialized AI application courses (Kong et al., 2023).

The relationship between self-efficacy and AI is highly significant, as self-effi- cacy is considered a key factor influencing students’ willingness to utilize AI tools and engage in AI learning. Educational interventions that enhance self-efficacy have been shown to increase students’ willingness to use AI tools and improve their learn- ing outcomes. A positive correlation exists between self-efficacy and students’ aca- demic achievements and performance (Zhang et al., 2024). AI technologies have the potential to foster students’ creativity, and the application of AI technologies, such as ChatGPT, has been found to enhance students’ creative thinking and design skills (Huang & Society, 2024). However, despite the innovative solutions and problem- solving techniques offered by AI technologies, challenges that limit students’ creativ- ity and innovation also persist (Lin & Chen, 2024). Furthermore, research indicates that the application of AI technologies can improve students’ academic achievements 

and performance (Lee et al., 2022; Shahzad et al., 2024). Self-efficacy and creativ- ity are regarded as mediating variables in the relationship between AI technologies and learning outcomes (Shahzad et al., 2024). Educational interventions enhanced by AI, such as the use of AI chatbots, have the potential to improve students’ academic achievements (Lee et al., 2022).

While existing research has explored the direct effects of variables such as AI lit- eracy, self-efficacy, and creativity on student development, few studies have compre- hensively examined the indirect effects among these variables, or have focused solely on the interactions of one or two of them. Additionally, current studies predominantly employ traditional statistical analysis methods, such as regression analysis or path analysis, which may have limitations in addressing the complex relationships and nonlinear patterns among variables (O’Brien & Silcox, 2024; Vulic et al., 2024). Therefore, this research will integrate Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to investigate the relationships among these variables using more advanced methodolo- gies, aiming to provide a more comprehensive understanding of student learning and AI education.

**3 Model conceptualization and hypotheses development**

This study presents a conceptual model that is informed by the Cognitive Behavioral Theory (CBT) framework. Within this model, AI literacy and creativity are identified as pivotal components of the cognitive dimension, self-efficacy is categorized under the affective dimension, and academic achievement is incorporated into the behav- ioral dimension. The study seeks to elucidate the influences across these dimensions, thereby validating the interplay between college students’ AI literacy, creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement. Furthermore, the model encompasses the dynamic interactions within the cognitive domain, such as the potential for AI lit- eracy to enhance creativity (see Fig. 1). The construction of this model is grounded in the broad acceptance of theoretical underpinnings and the escalating significance of AI literacy and creativity in contemporary education and learning. It underscores the imperative for the educational sector to foster individuals’ AI literacy and creativity, aspiring to offer a theoretical foundation and guidance for educational practices of the future.

**3.1 Artificial intelligence literacy**

In the current research landscape, AI literacy is widely regarded as a crucial factor influencing individuals’ self-efficacy, academic achievement, and creativity. Al-Abd- ullatif and Alsubaie ([2024)](#declarations) conducted an analysis using structural equation model- ing, revealing that students with higher levels of AI literacy are more inclined to recognize the value of AI tools such as ChatGPT, which enhances their confidence in utilizing these tools (Ning et al., 2025a). This finding is further corroborated by Lee et al. (2022), who discovered that the use of AI chatbots not only improves students’ academic performance but also boosts their self-efficacy. Additionally, the frame-

work proposed by Yu and Wu (2021), based on recurrent neural networks, demon- strates that the application of AI technologies in education can effectively enhance students’ academic achievements. Furthermore, Lin and Chen (2024) indicated that AI-integrated educational applications can stimulate students’ creativity by introduc- ing new ideas and problem-solving techniques. Accordingly, the study proposed that:

Hypothesis 1: Artificial intelligence literacy positively affects self-efficacy; Hypothesis 2: Artificial intelligence literacy positively affects academic achievement; Hypothesis 3: Artificial intelligence literacy positively affects creativity.

Research by Chen et al. ([2024a)](#declarations), grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model, has illuminated how AI self-efficacy can influence students’ engagement with AI tools by mitigating AI-related anxiety and fostering more positive attitudes toward AI, potentially leading to enhanced academic achievements.(Mamlok, 2024), from a theoretical and conceptual vantage point, has discussed the repercussions of integrat- ing AI in education, highlighting the importance of elevating students’ understanding and utilization of AI tools to strengthen their self-efficacy, which may subsequently improve learning outcomes. Huang and Society (2024) have shown through a digital game development initiative that generative AI-supported co-regulated learning can markedly boost students’ creativity and design thinking, indirectly impacting their academic achievements. Andriopoulos et al. ([2018)](#declarations) have examined, at the team level, the influence of AI literacy on self-efficacy through the enhancement of team creativ- ity. Accordingly, the study proposed that:

Hypothesis 4: The effect of artificial intelligence literacy on academic achievement is mediated by self-efficacy;

Hypothesis 5: The effect of artificial intelligence literacy on academic achievement is mediated by creativity;

Hypothesis 6: The effect of artificial intelligence literacy on self-efficacy is mediated by creativity.

**3.2 Creativity**

The nexus between creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement is increas- ingly under the academic microscope. A study by Urban et al. (2024) employed experimental methodologies to assess the influence of ChatGPT on the performance of college students in addressing intricate creative challenges. The findings demon- strated that engagement with ChatGPT notably amplified students’ self-efficacy, a discovery that affirms the constructive role of heightened creativity in strengthening one’s self-efficacy.

Jauk (2019) introduced a “bio-psycho-behavioral” framework to elucidate the con- cept of creativity. This framework underscores the pivotal role of cognitive creative potential and intelligence in manifesting real-world creativity across various domains. It corroborates the positive influence of creativity on academic achievement, suggest- ing that creativity is a critical cognitive dimension in shaping educational outcomes. In the research conducted by Zhang et al. (2022a), the interplay between retrieval flexibility and creativity was scrutinized using computational linguistics metrics. The study revealed that retrieval flexibility is positively associated with multiple behav- ioral constructs of creativity, potentially fostering distinctive search patterns within different creative cohorts and directly impacting academic achievement. Karataş et al. (2024) delved into the utilization of ChatGPT in foreign language instruction through qualitative case studies. The research indicated that ChatGPT not only positively influenced students’ creativity but also augmented their self-effi- cacy, prompting the researchers to hypothesize an indirect enhancement of academic achievement. Accordingly, the study proposed that:

Hypothesis 7: Creativity positively affects self-efficacy; Hypothesis 8: Creativity positively affects academic achievement;

Hypothesis 9: The effect of creativity on academic achievement is mediated by self-efficacy.

**3.3 Self-efficacy**

Self-efficacy, defined as an individual’s conviction in their capability to accomplish specific tasks (Bandura, [1977)](#declarations), is intricately linked to academic achievement within the realms of education and psychology. Research conducted by Chang et al. ([2022)](#declarations) demonstrated that the integration of mobile chatbots into the learning process can bolster the academic achievement and self-efficacy of nursing students, thereby sug- gesting that an enhancement in self-efficacy directly amplifies students’ academic performance. The research conducted by Wang and Li (2024) extended the Expec- tation-Confirmation Model (ECM) by integrating cognitive and affective variables to assess the current state of AI utilization among college students and their future expectations. The results indicated that digital self-efficacy and positive emotions significantly impact the continued use of AI, with positive emotions emerging as especially pivotal. Furthermore, self-efficacy was found to have a direct influence on both the adoption of learning technologies and the attainment of academic success. Accordingly, the study proposed that:

Hypothesis 10: Self-efficacy positively affects academic achievement.

**4 Methodology**

**4.1 Instrument**

Given the presence of latent variables that are not directly observable in this research, scales have been developed for their measurement. The AI literacy questionnaire has been adapted from Mikalef and Gupta (2021). To reliably gauge the levels of creativ- ity among college students, the subjective measurement of creativity was adapted from Williams (1979), Liu et al. (2016) and the objective measurement was derived from “The Test for Creative Thinking-Drawing Production” (TCT-DP) (Jellen & Urban, 1986; Urban, 2005). By amalgamating subjective and objective data, a holis- tic representation of students’ actual creative performance is captured, which in turn bolsters the credibility of the study (For specific empirical findings, refer to Appendix 1, Figs. 2, 3, 4 and 5). The measurement of self-efficacy was adapted from Schwarzer (1997), and that of academic achievement from (Al-Rahmi et al., [2021)](#declarations). These con- structs were assessed using a Likert scale that spans from 1 (“strongly disagree”) to 5 (“strongly agree”), and a pilot study was undertaken to evaluate the quality of the questionnaire (McGill & Klobas, 2009). To ensure that participants could compre- hend and complete the questionnaire and practical tests with precision, a pilot survey was conducted with the involvement of 20 university students, educators, adminis- trators, and scholars possessing pertinent research experience. Their insights led to the refinement of certain items and execution protocols, resulting in a questionnaire 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 2** Results of the research model devoid of potential ambiguities, imprecise phrasing, or items that were challenging to grasp (see Appendix 2 Table [9)](#appendix-2), complemented by the TCT-DP-based creativity practical test. Ultimately, all constructs achieved a Cronbach’s α greater than 0.7, and the concordance between objective and subjective creativity data surpassed 80%, attesting to the reliability of the measurements. 

**4.2 Sample and data collection**

Several universities in China have initiated efforts to enhance students’ proficiency in AI and foster their creativity. This initiative is designed to predict students’ emo- tional states, academic achievements, and to offer tailored learning suggestions (Lin & Chen, 2024). The purposive (judgment) sampling technique is known to augment the theoretical soundness and reliability of research outcomes (Sharma, 2017; Uzir et al., 2021). Furthermore, this method eases the process of participant recruitment and data collection (Campbell et al., [2020;](#declarations) Salloum et al., 2019) and has been exten- sively utilized in quantitative studies (Anggraeni & Sole, [2020;](#declarations) Pratama et al., 2020; Yustina, 2020).

In the context of this study, purposive sampling was used to ensure that the sample represents specific populations of interest, allowing us to focus on participants who are most likely to provide data on the interplay among AI literacy, creativity, self- efficacy, and academic achievement. Moreover, purposive sampling enables the tar- geting of specific subgroups within the student population, such as those with high AI literacy but low creativity, or high self-efficacy but average academic performance, allowing us to explore these relationships in more detail than random sampling meth- ods. This sampling method is particularly suitable for mixed-methods research as it allows researchers to delve deeply into the phenomenon of interest while maintain- ing a manageable sample size (Palinkas et al., 2015). Consistent with the recom- mendations of Morse and Niehaus (2009), purposive sampling in this study aims to maximize efficiency and effectiveness. By selecting participants with knowledge and experience in using AI, we can obtain detailed and credible data that enhance the trustworthiness of the research findings and help achieve theoretical saturation, a point at which no new substantive information is obtained, ensuring that our sample is sufficiently comprehensive.

Therefore, for the successful attainment of this study’s objectives and the effec- tive execution of the survey, it is imperative that the schools of the participants have incorporated the application of AI technology into their educational frameworks. In particular, these institutions must have employed AI tools and platforms within their teaching and learning processes, actively adhered to and implemented guidelines for the use of AI in education, and offered a wide array of academic disciplines. Such measures are crucial to ensuring the broad applicability of the research outcomes. In terms of participant selection, students who have engaged with AI courses to a certain extent, utilized AI products, and demonstrated diverse academic achievement levels were targeted. Using purposive (judgment) sampling, this study identified three Chinese universities that met the aforementioned criteria. These universities were selected due to their integration of AI tools and platforms into their teaching processes, as well as their diverse student bodies encompassing various academic 

disciplines and degree levels (bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral). To ensure that the sample comprehensively represented students with varying degrees of AI exposure and academic performance, teachers who taught AI-related courses or were familiar with the use of AI tools in education were invited to participate in the data collec- tion process. These teachers were able to effectively communicate the purpose of the survey to the students and guide their participation. They were instructed to recruit students who had either taken AI courses or used AI products to ensure that the par- ticipants had a certain level of understanding of AI concepts. Additionally, efforts were made to include students from different academic years to capture the varying stages of AI literacy, creativity, self-efficacy, and academic performance throughout their university education.

During the data collection process, the questionnaire was distributed through mul- tiple channels, including classes, WeChat groups, QQ groups, and email. The ques- tionnaire was developed on the Wenjuanxing platform, which offers functionalities similar to Amazon’s Mechanical Turk, facilitating the creation and distribution of QR codes and survey invitation links. Teachers announced the survey in class and on the questionnaire, explaining its purpose and significance, emphasizing the voluntary nature of participation and confidentiality. Students were informed that the survey was conducted in an anonymous self-report format and that no personal information would be disclosed. After class, teachers shared the QR code for the questionnaire via WeChat and QQ groups to reach students who could not attend the class announce- ment. Additionally, teachers sent survey invitations via email, providing the survey link and a brief overview of the study. These methods ensured that students had mul- tiple opportunities to access the survey.

To ensure informed participation, students were provided with detailed informa- tion about the survey’s purpose, the estimated time required to complete it, and their right to withdraw at any stage of the survey. This comprehensive approach to partici- pant information was designed to ensure that all participants were fully aware of the study’s nature and could voluntarily contribute to the research. Data collection lasted for four weeks, during which we received a total of 434 responses.

Following the completion of data collection, questionnaires with excessively short response times or consistent answers were excluded. The univariate outliers within the dataset were then identified by computing the standardized scores for each case (Goodboy & Kline, 2017). The presence of multivariate outliers was assessed using the Mahalanobis distance (Mahalanobis, 1936). To ensure the statistical validity of the outlier detection, a significance test with _p_ \< 0.001 was performed. Subsequently, all identified outliers were removed, yielding a final sample of 385 cases, represent- ing an effectiveness rate of 88.71% for further analysis (Abu Al Aish & Love, [2013)](#declarations). The demographic characteristics of the final sample are broken down as follows: In terms of gender, 181 participants (47%) were male, and 204 participants (53%) were female. Regarding educational background, 174 participants (45%) were Bachelor’s Degree Students, 108 participants (28%) were Master’s Degree Students, and 103 participants (27%) were Ph.D. students. These diverse demographic characteristics of the respondents contribute to the richness of the data and the potential generaliz- ability of the findings within the context of college students with different educational levels and genders (see Table 1).

Due to the reliance on a single source of self-reported surveys for data collec- tion in this study, the possibility of common method bias (CMB) was examined in accordance with Podsakoff et al. (2003). To test for CMB, this study employed two techniques: Harman’s single-factor test and the full collinearity test (Kock & Lynn, 2012). Harman’s single-factor test revealed that the initial factor accounted for only 31.9% of the variance, which is below the threshold of 40%. The results of the full collinearity test indicated that all structural variance inflation factors (VIF) were below the recommended threshold of 3. Consequently, it can be inferred that CMB does not pose a significant issue in this study (see Table 2).

However, it is acknowledged that the use of purposive sampling may introduce potential biases. One potential bias is the selection bias, as the participants were chosen based on specific criteria related to AI exposure and academic performance. This could limit the generalizability of the findings to the broader college student population who may not have had similar AI-related experiences. Another potential bias is the non-response bias. Although the response rate was relatively high, those who chose to participate may have had more interest or positive attitudes towards AI, which could skew the results. To mitigate these biases, future research could consider using random sampling methods or expanding the recruitment scope to include a wider range of universities and student populations with different backgrounds.

**4.3 Data analysis**

This study is exploratory, aiming to understand the relationships among the four vari- ables of AI literacy, creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement, and to iden- tify factors that can predict academic achievement. To achieve these objectives, the study employs a mixed-methods approach, utilizing both PLS-SEM and fsQCA for data analysis. Given the exploratory and complex nature of the model, PLS-SEM was chosen for its robustness in predicting complex models (Hair et al., 2019; Iranmanesh et al., 2022) Additionally, fsQCA was employed to better understand the relationships between these factors.

FsQCA is suitable for this study for several reasons. First, traditional regression methods, including PLS-SEM, have limitations in capturing complex causal relation- ships, whereas fsQCA is specifically designed to identify multiple pathways (con- figurations) that lead to the same outcome (Fiss, 2007). This capability is crucial for understanding the interplay among the variables in this study. In contrast, multi- group SEM, which shares some similarities with fsQCA, is primarily used to vali-

date existing theoretical assumptions rather than to explore new theoretical pathways (Deng & Yuan, 2015). Interaction modeling, while capable of capturing interaction effects between two variables, is typically limited to pairwise interactions and is less effective in handling multiple conditions and their combinations (Porter et al., 1994). Second, fsQCA can capture asymmetric relationships, where the presence of a condition may be sufficient to cause an outcome, but its absence may not be neces- sary for the absence of the outcome. This feature allows fsQCA to effectively analyze the necessary conditions influencing students’ creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement. Multi-group SEM, on the other hand, is mainly used to compare path coefficient differences between groups, assuming linear relationships between vari- ables and thus failing to capture complex non-linear relationships accurately (Byrne, [2010)](#declarations).

Third, fsQCA is appropriate for small to medium-sized samples (Ragin, 1989), which is typical for exploratory research. In contrast, multi-group SEM and interac- tion modeling generally require larger sample sizes to ensure model stability and reliability (Marsh et al., 2004; Porter et al., 1994). The following sections provide a comprehensive explanation of the results obtained from both methods.

**5 Result**

**5.1 Symmetric analysis**

**5.1.1 Measurement model assessment**

The measurement model was evaluated using PLS-SEM with the collected question- naire data. Random sampling was performed in SmartPLS 4, with a sample size of 5,000. The model examines the interrelationships among AI literacy, creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement (see Fig. 6). The assessment included indi- cator loadings, composite reliability (CR), and average variance extracted (AVE). As shown in Table 2, all item loadings exceeded the recommended threshold of 0.7, and all constructs achieved satisfactory AVE values (\> 0.5) and CR values (\> 0.7) (For- oughi et al., 2022). Discriminant validity was confirmed by calculating the Hetero- trait-Monotrait (HTMT) ratio, with all values below the threshold of 0.85 (Foroughi et al., 2023; Henseler et al., 2015), indicating adequate discriminant validity (see Table 3).

**5.1.2 Structural model assessment**

The structural model (see Fig. 6) was assessed using the R² (coefficient of determi- nation) values for creativity (0.121), self-efficacy (0.160), and academic achieve- ment (0.255). These values indicate that the model explains 25.5% of the variance in academic achievement. The results show significant direct effects of AI literacy (β = 0.281; _p_ \< 0.01), creativity (β = 0.172; _p_ \< 0.01), and self-efficacy (β = 0.211; _p_ \< 0.01) on academic achievement (see Table 4). Additionally, AI literacy significantly influences self-efficacy (β = 0.252; _p_ \< 0.01) and creativity (β = 0.349; _p_ \< 0.01), while creativity also significantly impacts self-efficacy (β = 0.235; _p_ \< 0.01). The model evaluates two mediating pathways involving self-efficacy and creativ- ity. In the pathway where self-efficacy serves as a mediator, both the direct and indi- rect effects of AI literacy and creativity on academic achievement are significant, indicating that self-efficacy partially mediates these relationships. Similarly, in the pathway where creativity acts as a mediator, both the direct and indirect effects of AI

**5.2 Asymmetric analysis**

To address the limitations of PLS-SEM in capturing the nonlinear relationships between factors influencing academic achievement, self-efficacy, and creativity, we employed fsQCA to examine the synergistic effects of multiple factors on outcomes (Ning et al., 2025b). fsQCA identifies configurations or combinations of factors that effectively achieve significant levels of these outcomes, rather than focusing on indi- vidual predictors (Fiss, 2011). Additionally, necessity analyses were conducted to determine if any single factor is crucial for achieving high levels of these outcomes (Dul, 2016). A configuration is considered sufficient if its consistency and coverage values are at least 0.8 and 0.2, respectively, while a necessary condition requires both values to exceed 0.9 (Dul, 2016; Ragin, 2008).

The fsQCA analysis followed a standard procedure: data calibration, truth table construction, and causal condition analysis (Ragin, 2017). Raw data were trans- formed into fuzzy sets based on Likert scale thresholds for full membership (0.95), cross-over anchors (0.50), and full non-membership (0.05) (Kallmuenzer et al., 2019). The calibrated data were then input into fsQCA 4.1 software to generate a truth table. The fuzzy set representing the impact of three condition variables—AI

This aligns with existing theories that AI literacy encompasses critical thinking, problem-solving, and innovative capabilities, which are foundational to the development of creativity.

**6 Discussion**

**6.1 Findings of symmetric approach (PLS-SEM)**

The current study indicates that AI literacy can significantly enhance students’ self-efficacy. This finding aligns with previous research, such as that conducted by Al-Abdullatif and Alsubaie ([2024)](#declarations) and Lee et al. (2022). The advancement of AI technology has led to the gradual integration of AI literacy into various aspects of social life. As students gain increased confidence in their abilities when using digital devices or systems, their enhanced self-efficacy empowers them to approach tasks with greater confidence. This suggests that AI literacy is a critical component in modern education, enabling students to navigate and succeed in a technology-driven world.

The results of this study also confirm the positive correlation between AI literacy and academic achievement in the era of AI, aligning with findings from previous studies such as those by Yu and Wu (2021) and Lee et al. (2022). AI technologies, par- ticularly generative AI systems, can efficiently process and understand vast amounts of data, thereby enhancing the efficiency and speed of knowledge production. This transformation offers new possibilities for the intelligent and informatized develop- ment of higher education. Additionally, many universities worldwide have conducted beneficial explorations in the application of AI in classrooms, providing more oppor- tunities for the diverse development of educational resources. To address the chal- lenges posed by AI to society, universities need to cultivate comprehensive abilities in college students that are required in the age of AI, including understanding, using, 

and innovating with AI. Enhancing these abilities can help students choose appropri- ate learning paths and methods, thereby improving their academic achievement. The significant impact of AI literacy on creativity aligns with the findings of stud- ies conducted by Lin and Chen (2024) and Huang and Society (2024). AI literacy emphasizes the ability to embrace new technologies and foster a spirit of exploration, encouraging students to continually consider how to apply AI technologies to solve real-world problems, thereby stimulating greater innovation. When confronted with new technologies, developing AI literacy through the exercise of analytical, evalua- tive, reasoning, and judgment skills helps students think independently when apply- ing AI technologies, enhancing their creativity. This suggests that AI literacy not only improves technical skills but also fosters a mindset conducive to innovation. The positive impact of creativity on self-efficacy is consistent with the findings of Urban et al. (2024), who observed that using ChatGPT significantly enhances stu- dents’ self-efficacy. When students achieve success through creative activities, these experiences bolster their self-efficacy. Thus, the successful experiences gained from creative activities become one of the key sources of enhanced self-efficacy. Addition- ally, the development of creativity often involves learning and mastering new skills. As students acquire new skills in creative tasks, they feel more competent, which in turn boosts their self-efficacy. In creative activities, students may also receive recog- nition and respect from their peers. This social validation and sense of belonging can further strengthen their self-efficacy.

This study supports the conclusion that creativity has a positive impact on aca- demic achievement, which is consistent with previous observations (Jauk, 2019; Zhang et al., 2022a). Creativity enables students to solve problems in novel and unique ways, encouraging them to break free from traditional thought patterns and seek innovative solutions. This approach allows for a better understanding and analy- sis of problems, leading to improved performance in learning. Moreover, creativity encourages students to apply knowledge to new contexts and problems, enhancing their ability to solidify and expand their knowledge base. By creatively utilizing their knowledge, students are better equipped to master the learning content and perform exceptionally well in exams and assessments. Additionally, creativity often involves interdisciplinary thinking, which helps students establish connections across differ- ent subjects and develop a more comprehensive knowledge system. This integrative ability allows them to understand and analyze problems from multiple perspectives, contributing to more holistic academic progress.

The research findings also indicate that self-efficacy significantly enhances stu- dents’ academic achievement. This discovery aligns with previous studies, such as those by Wang and Li (2024) and Chang et al. ([2022)](#declarations). When students have confidence in their abilities, they are more likely to set higher learning goals and exert effort to achieve them. Furthermore, students with high self-efficacy tend to view learning as a challenge rather than a threat, and this positive attitude helps them maintain sustained motivation for learning. Self-efficacy also influences the way students attribute their learning outcomes. Students with high self-efficacy are more inclined to attribute their successes to their own efforts and abilities rather than external factors such as luck. This positive attribution style aids students in persisting and striving when 

faced with difficulties. Such intrinsic beliefs enhance students’ resilience and ability to recover, ultimately leading to improved academic achievement.

Consistent with our initial expectations, the results indicate that both the direct and indirect effects of AI literacy on academic achievement are significant when medi- ated by self-efficacy, suggesting that self-efficacy partially mediates the impact of AI literacy on academic achievement (see Table 5). Enhancing AI literacy can increase students’ experiences of success, leading them to believe in their ability to achieve desired levels of accomplishment, thereby improving their self-efficacy. Students with stronger self-efficacy tend to evaluate their learning abilities more positively and are more likely to face academic stressors with a proactive attitude, viewing stress as a challenge and opportunity, which in turn leads to greater engagement in learn- ing. Additionally, as AI literacy boosts students’ self-efficacy, this enhanced self-effi- cacy can further improve academic achievement by influencing students’ learning motivation. Higher levels of academic self-efficacy result in students setting higher academic goals and placing greater importance on academic performance. Through these mechanisms, AI literacy influences students’ evaluations of their learning abili- ties, learning motivation, and engagement by enhancing self-efficacy, ultimately leading to improved academic achievement.

At the same time, self-efficacy functions as a mediating variable in the relation- ship between creativity and academic achievement, playing a partial mediating role in the influence of creativity on academic success. This study has previously estab- lished that creativity has a direct positive impact on self-efficacy, and that self-effi- cacy also directly influences academic achievement. Creativity enhances students’ self-efficacy through experiences of successful creative activities, mastery of new skills, and recognition from peers. This increased self-efficacy makes students more likely to set ambitious learning goals, maintain a positive attitude toward learning, and attribute their success to their own efforts and abilities, thereby improving aca- demic achievement.

In the pathway where creativity serves as a mediating variable, both the direct and indirect effects of AI literacy on academic achievement are significant, with cre- ativity playing a partial mediating role. This study has previously established that AI literacy positively influences creativity, which in turn has a positive impact on academic achievement. AI literacy emphasizes the acceptance and exploration of new technologies, encouraging students to apply AI technologies to solve real-world problems, thereby stimulating their creativity. This stimulated creativity enables stu- dents to approach problem-solving in novel and unique ways, breaking free from traditional thought patterns to seek innovative solutions and establish connections across different disciplines, ultimately forming a more comprehensive knowledge system. Such capabilities contribute to improved academic performance. Moreover, creativity also acts as a mediating variable in the relationship between AI literacy and self-efficacy, playing a partial mediating role in the influence of AI lit- eracy on self-efficacy (see Table 5). The results of this study have demonstrated that AI literacy significantly impacts creativity, which in turn has a notable effect on self- efficacy. AI literacy encourages students to embrace new technologies and explore their applications in solving real-world problems, thereby stimulating their creativity. This enhanced creativity subsequently boosts students’ self-efficacy through experi-

ences of successful creative activities, mastery of new skills, and recognition from peers.

**6.2 Findings of asymmetric approach (fsQCA results)**

The fsQCA reveals the complex interplay among AI literacy, creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement by identifying multiple configurations. Unlike the PLS- SEM model, which offers a single optimization model with an explanatory power of 25.5%, fsQCA uncovers five distinct configurations that collectively account for 75.1% of the variance in these outcomes. This higher explanatory power indicates that students follow diverse learning paths and emphases, which a single model can- not fully capture.

The fsQCA results highlight AI literacy as a core condition in all effective con- figurations, consistent with the PLS-SEM findings, further confirming its significant impact on academic performance, self-efficacy, and creativity. Additionally, fsQCA shows that students choose different paths to influence their academic achievement based on their preferences and needs. For example, in Configuration 1 (AIL\*CRE), students enhance their AI literacy and creativity to achieve high academic perfor- mance; in Configuration 2 (AIL\*SE), they focus on improving AI literacy and self- efficacy; while in Configuration 3 (CRE\*SE), students opt to boost creativity and self-efficacy for academic success.

Notably, the combination of creativity and self-efficacy in Configuration 3 exhibits high consistency but low coverage, suggesting that this combination may influence academic achievement under specific conditions. Specifically, when both creativity and self-efficacy are present, their impact on academic achievement is stable, but this combination is not universally present in all cases. This indicates that the influ- ence of creativity and self-efficacy on academic achievement may be more context- dependent, emphasizing the importance of fostering these traits through supportive learning environments and innovative teaching methods.

In Configuration 4 (AIL\*CRE), the influence of high AI literacy and high creativ- ity on self-efficacy aligns with the PLS-SEM findings, showing that creativity medi- ates the relationship between AI literacy and self-efficacy. Together, they enhance students’ self-efficacy, further supporting the interconnectivity of these variables. In Configuration 5 (AIL), AI literacy alone shows high coverage and consistency in its impact on creativity, indicating that AI literacy can largely explain creativity. In summary, the combined analysis of PLS-SEM and fsQCA demonstrates a high degree of consistency in the relationships between AI literacy, creativity, self-effi- cacy, and academic achievement. While PLS-SEM provides a comprehensive view of the direct and indirect effects of these variables, fsQCA reveals the diverse con- figurations through which they interact to produce significant outcomes. This inte- grated approach offers a more nuanced understanding of the factors contributing to academic success in the context of AI literacy.

**6.3 Cross-cultural implications and generalizability of the findings**

This study has focused on Chinese college students, providing insights into the rela- tionships among AI literacy, creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement. However, extending these findings to other educational systems and cultural contexts requires further analysis and validation. The impact of AI literacy on student devel- opment varies across different cultural backgrounds. In individualistic cultures, AI is often perceived as an external tool, with certain characteristics potentially viewed as potential threats to individual uniqueness, autonomy, and privacy (Kwak et al., 2022). In contrast, in collectivist cultures like China, the collective benefits and application values of AI are more emphasized (Zhang et al., 2023). These cultural differences may influence students’ perceptions and applications of AI literacy, thereby affecting its relationships with self-efficacy and academic achievement.

Despite the positive correlation between creativity and academic achievement across various contexts, the cultivation and emphasis on creativity differ across cultures. Some Western educational systems tend to foster creativity through open- ended projects and interdisciplinary problem-solving tasks (Gajda et al., 2016), while the Chinese educational system places greater emphasis on integrating creativity into the curriculum (Knox, 2020). These differences may lead to variations in the inter- play between creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement across cultures. As an important mediating variable, self-efficacy is also influenced by cultural factors. In collectivist cultures, self-efficacy is more closely linked to group achievements and social support, whereas in individualistic cultures, it focuses more on personal accomplishments. These cultural differences may affect the mediating role of self- efficacy between AI literacy, creativity, and academic achievement. For example, in collectivist cultures, students with higher self-efficacy may be more motivated to participate in team AI projects, thereby enhancing academic performance (Dai et al., 2019). In individualistic cultures, self-efficacy may drive students to pursue personal AI learning paths and creative activities, leading to academic success (Naiseh et al., 2025).

When extending the findings of this study to other contexts, it is essential to con- sider the specific educational systems and cultural backgrounds. Although AI literacy, creativity, and self-efficacy have certain impacts on academic achievement among Chinese college students, further research is needed to validate the applicability of these findings in other environments. For instance, in countries with different edu- cational policies and resources, the impact of AI literacy on academic achievement may be influenced by the availability and quality of AI education programs (Yim & Su, 2025). Additionally, varying cultural attitudes toward education and technology may shape the relationships among these variables (Ma et al., 2024a). In summary, this study provides insights into the relationships among AI literacy, creativity, self- efficacy, and academic achievement among Chinese college students. However, cau- tion is needed when applying these findings to other educational systems and cultural contexts. Future research should conduct cross-cultural comparisons and take into account the unique characteristics of different educational environments to better understand the generalizability of these relationships.

**7 Theoretical and practical implications**

**7.1 Theoretical implications**

This study provides new empirical evidence regarding the relationships among AI literacy, creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement among college students. Although previous research has examined the individual effects of these variables, a systematic analysis of their interrelationships has been lacking. By integrating PLS- SEM and fsQCA methodologies, this study not only elucidates how AI literacy, cre- ativity, and self-efficacy influence academic achievement but also investigates the interactions among these three factors. This comprehensive exploration enhances the generalizability of the findings and offers a new theoretical foundation for educa- tional practice.

Second, this study has developed a comprehensive model based on cognitive- behavioral theory, integrating four variables—AI literacy, creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement—into a single analytical framework. The construction of this theoretical framework provides a solid foundation for understanding the core competencies required of college students in the era of AI, emphasizing the impor- tance for educators to prioritize the development of students’ AI literacy and creativ- ity. Furthermore, the model established in this study offers a basis for subsequent research to validate and expand upon, thereby advancing the development of related theories. It also provides a new perspective for innovative practices in the field of education, laying a theoretical foundation for cultivating individuals who can meet the demands of future society.

Third, by integrating subjective data obtained from questionnaire surveys with objective data measured by the TCT-DP, this study provides a comprehensive basis for observing college students’ creativity. Traditional research methods often focus on a single data source, which may lead to biased assessments of students’ creativ- ity. In this study, subjective feedback regarding creativity was collected from stu- dents through questionnaires, reflecting their inner feelings and personal perceptions, thus offering direct insights into their intrinsic motivations and psychological states. Simultaneously, the inclusion of objective data from the TCT-DP provides external, quantifiable indicators for assessing students’ creativity. By combining these subjec- tive and objective data analyses, this research captures the multidimensional char- acteristics of college students’ creativity more comprehensively, resulting in more accurate measurement outcomes. This approach not only enhances the reliability of the study but also offers more targeted guidance for educational practice, helping educators better understand and support the development of students’ creativity. Fourth, the theoretical contribution of this study includes the identification of psy- chological and cognitive factors that influence students’ academic achievement. This provides educators with a basis for adjusting teaching methods and content according to the specific needs and abilities of each student. By understanding the differences among students in AI literacy, creativity, and self-efficacy, educators can design more targeted instructional strategies. This recognition and respect for individual differ- ences can more effectively stimulate each student’s learning potential and promote their development.

**7.2 Practical implications**

In the context of the rapid advancement of AI technologies, universities should actively take on the responsibility of promoting AI literacy. By offering a variety of formats such as open courses, seminars, and online classes, universities can not only enhance the public’s understanding and awareness of AI but also stimulate greater enthusiasm among students and various sectors of society to engage in AI learning. Such outreach activities help to increase societal emphasis on AI literacy, thereby laying a foundation for the cultivation of more professional talent.

This study emphasizes the integration of AI education into university curricula, encompassing aspects such as foundational knowledge, technological applications, and innovation capabilities. Higher education institutions should incorporate AI as a core course, with the goal of cultivating students’ AI literacy. This curriculum inte- gration not only helps students understand the potential and limitations of AI tech- nologies but also prepares them adequately for their future careers. Through carefully designed courses, students can acquire essential technical skills while also develop- ing critical thinking and problem-solving abilities, which are crucial for adapting to rapidly changing learning and work environments.

In addition, given the significant impact of creativity and self-efficacy on aca- demic achievement, this study suggests that educators should adopt more interactive and student-centered teaching methods to stimulate students’ creativity and enhance their self-efficacy. Approaches such as project-based learning, problem-based learn- ing, and collaborative learning can effectively encourage students to actively explore, solve problems, and learn through practice. These teaching methods not only aid in the development of independent thinking and collaboration skills but also lay a solid foundation for their future academic and professional success.

Self-efficacy is closely related to students’ mental health; therefore, higher educa- tion institutions should provide necessary psychological support and academic guid- ance services to help students build confidence, manage academic stress, and prepare for future learning and career development. Through mental health education and stress management workshops, students can learn effective strategies for coping with challenges and adversity. Furthermore, universities should establish a supportive learning environment that encourages mutual assistance and collaboration among students, thereby enhancing their social support networks.

The research findings provide important evidence for educational policymakers, promoting student-centered educational reforms. Policymakers can utilize these find- ings to develop relevant policies that foster the advancement of AI education and enhance the quality and equity of education. Such policies may include funding allo- cations, teacher training, curriculum development, and reforms in assessment sys- tems. Additionally, policymakers should consider how to improve teaching efficiency and learning outcomes through educational technology, as well as how to ensure that all students have access to high-quality educational opportunities through equi- table education policies. Through these reforms, a greater number of individuals with innovative and practical skills can be cultivated, contributing positively to social and economic development.

**8 Limitations and future research**

This study acknowledges certain limitations and shortcomings, aiming to provide direction for future research endeavors. Firstly, the research sample was limited to Chinese students and employed purposive (judgment) sampling. Therefore, it is rec- ommended that future research examines the study model in different geographical locations and adopts more diverse sampling methods to enhance the generalizability of the findings. This study has identified cognitive-behavioral theory as the theo- retical foundation for analyzing the relationships between AI literacy, creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement. Future research is encouraged to explore additional theoretical perspectives, such as Social Cognitive Theory (SCT), Self- Determination Theory (SDT), COM-B model(Capability, Opportunity, Motivation, and Behavior Model), and Social Support Theory (SST), to further our understanding of the relationships among these four variables.

Secondly, this study primarily relies on questionnaire surveys and objective mea- surements of only the creativity variable, which may introduce common method bias. Although measures have been taken to control for this bias and statistical tests have not detected any issues related to common method bias, the subjectivity of question- naire data may still affect the accuracy of the research findings. To enhance the reli- ability and validity of the study, future research could incorporate additional objective data sources, such as students’ academic transcripts and teacher evaluations. Integrat- ing diverse data sources will help to more comprehensively capture students’ actual performance, thereby increasing the credibility of the research.

Thirdly, this study employed a cross-sectional design. While cross-sectional stud- ies can provide insights into the correlations between variables, they cannot reveal causal effects over time. Future research could adopt a longitudinal design to track changes in students at different time points, thereby more accurately uncovering the dynamic relationships and causal effects between variables. For instance, by conduct- ing longitudinal surveys on the same group of students over different semesters or academic years, focusing on their AI literacy, creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement, researchers can gain a clearer understanding of the causal pathways among these variables. This approach would provide more targeted guidance for edu- cational practices.

Moreover, the R² values for creativity (0.121), self-efficacy (0.160), and academic achievement (0.255) suggests the presence of unmeasured confounders that could be influencing these constructs. One potential confounder is socioeconomic status (SES). Research has shown that SES significantly impacts academic achievement and creativity through various pathways, such as access to resources and parental involvement (Sirin, 2005). Similarly, positive teacher–student relationships enhance academic achievement by boosting self-efficacy and effective learning strategies (Ma et al., 2018). Peer influence, particularly the socioeconomic status of peers, also shapes students’ attitudes and behaviors, thereby affecting their academic outcomes (Ewijk & Sleegers, 2010).Cognitive activation in the classroom, which promotes critical thinking and problem-solving skills, may further mediate these relation- ships (Liu et al., 2024). Future studies may consider incorporating these factors into 

the model for analysis as control variables or intermediary variables to enhance the explanatory power of the model.

Finally, while this study offers insights into the positive impact of AI literacy on college students’ creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement, a critical examination of the limitations and potential drawbacks of AI literacy in education is still warranted. AI literacy is widely regarded as beneficial for students’ academic and career development. However, the rapid integration of AI technologies into edu- cational settings may result in students becoming overly reliant on AI tools. This over-reliance on automated solutions could potentially undermine students’ critical thinking and problem-solving skills (Regan & Jesse, 2019). Moreover, ethical issues surrounding AI, such as algorithmic bias and data privacy concerns, may have unin- tended consequences for students’ learning experiences and their perceptions of fair- ness and justice (Smith, 2020). Unequal access to AI education also poses the risk of exacerbating existing inequalities, as students from disadvantaged backgrounds may have limited opportunities to engage with and acquire AI literacy (Regan & Steeves, 2019). Future research should address these limitations and drawbacks by exploring strategies to mitigate the negative impacts of AI literacy and ensuring that its benefits are accessible to all students. This may involve developing AI education programs that emphasize ethical considerations, critical thinking, and equitable access, as well as examining the comprehensive impact of AI literacy on students’ long-term cogni- tive and social development. By undertaking these efforts, the academic community can better understand how to leverage the potential of AI literacy while minimizing its risks and ensuring a balanced and inclusive educational experience.

**9 Conclusion**

This study empirically investigates the relationships among college students’ AI lit- eracy, creativity, self-efficacy, and academic achievement, revealing the complex interactions among these variables and their significant impact on student learn- ing outcomes. Based on cognitive-behavioral theory, data were collected from 385 students and analyzed using a combination of PLS-SEM and fsQCA methods. The PLS results indicate that AI literacy not only directly influences students’ academic achievement but also indirectly enhances it by boosting self-efficacy and creativ- ity. Furthermore, AI literacy directly affects self-efficacy and indirectly promotes it through increased creativity. Creativity, in turn, directly influences students’ aca- demic achievement and indirectly enhances it by strengthening self-efficacy. Additionally, the fsQCA results suggest that students’ academic achievement and self-efficacy are determined by a combination of multiple factors rather than a sin- gle factor. By identifying five distinct configurations, the fsQCA analysis highlights effective combinations of factors that promote students’ academic achievement, self- efficacy, and creativity. The results also confirm the central role of AI literacy in all effective configurations, further validating its critical function in enhancing academic achievement, self-efficacy, and creativity. This study not only provides empirical sup- port for understanding the core competencies required by college students in the age of AI but also offers practical recommendations for educational practices aimed at cultivating talents that meet the demands of future society.
